name: Moroccan Style Salmon with Olives and Preserved Lemon
ingredients:
1 lb. Fresh Salmon Fillet
4 Tablespoons Extra Virgin Olive Oil
4 Tablespoons Ras El Hanout
1 Medium Yellow Onion, Diced
1 Cup Chicken or Vegetable Stock
1 Cup Water
1 Preserved Lemon
½ Cup of Olives of Your Choice (I used a mix of Cerignola, Manzanilla, and Kalamata)
¼ Cup Chopped Fresh Flat Leaf Parsley
¼ Cup Toasted Pine Nuts
directions:
Sprinkle two tablespoons of Ras El Hanout onto the flesh side of the salmon fillet.

Meanwhile, lightly toast the pine nuts in a dry skillet. Set aside.

Slice the olives in half (if already pitted). If they have pits, cut the fruit off of the pit. Set aside.

Remove the pulp from the center of the preserved lemon and rinse under cool water. Divide the preserved lemon into its four quadrants, and slice each quadrant into thin strips. Set aside.

Heat two tablespoons of olive oil over medium heat in a large skillet or tajine. Saute the diced onion until translucent. Remove the onions and set aside.

Heat the remaining two tablespoons of olive oil in the same skillet or tajine over high heat until very hot. Add the salmon fillet flesh side down. If the salmon fillet is too long to fit within the pan, you can cut it in half to fit. Cook for several minutes, until the Ras El Hanout becomes toasted and fragrant, and a crust forms.

Invert the salmon fillet(s) so they are skin side down. Return the onions to the pan and the remaining two tablespoons of Ras El Hanout. Saute for several minutes until Ras El Hanout is fragrant and coats the sauted onion.

Sdd the stock and water and bring to a simmer. Sprinkle the olives and preserved lemon slices on top of the salmon. Reduce the heat to low and cover. Simmer until salmon is cooked through, about 20 minutes.

To Serve: Cut salmon into 4 ounce portions. Garnish with parsley and pine nuts, and serve over whole wheat couscous or brown rice.
notes:
MOROCCAN STYLE SALMON WITH OLIVES AND PRESERVED LEMON

Moroccan-Style-Salmon-with-Preserved-Lemon-and-Olives

In my quest to get to know North African styles of Mediterranean cuisine a bit better, I began eyeing various Moroccan Tajines. In the course of this quest I learned a few things. First, I’d always assumed that ‘tajine’ referred to a kind of North African stew flavored with Ras El Hanout, that spice mixture prominent in North African cookery with the strong notes of cinnamon that I, in my limited experience, associate with Moroccan food. But in fact a tajine is actually a cooking vessel, usually earthenware,  with a rather large, conical lid. Some of them are utilitarian in design (like those in the photo below), but others are quite ornate and beautiful.

Moroccan Tajines. Photo credit: Wiki-Commons. 
Moroccan Tajines. Photo by Wiki-Commons.
Dishes cooked in a tajine, like the Moroccan classic Chicken Tajine, thus take on the name of the vessel they were cooked in. If you’re interested, you can buy a pretty fancy tagine from Le Souk Ceramique (this is an affiliate link).

The second thing I learned when I began eyeing Moroccan Tajines is that you simply cannot get very far in cooking North African Mediterranean cuisine without preserved lemons. And since preserved lemons are not readily available for purchase (at least where I live), I eventually realized that I would need to suck it up and make my own. And recently I did. You can find the recipe here. And I’m so glad I did. They’re so incredibly intense and lemony that I can’t imagine not having a batch of them available in the refrigerator ever again. This recipe is the first to make use of them.

Salmon-rubbed-with-Moroccan-Spice

 

Some people are quite unyielding in their demand that specific dishes are to be prepared in the exacting fashion of the dish’s region of origin, using only ingredients from that region of origin. While I’m willing to meet these guardians of tradition halfway (I fermented a batch of preserved lemons after all), I have to confess that I’ve never really been a fan of this kind of exacting vehemence. To me it’s equivalent to turning something vibrant and alive into a museum piece. I find it much more interesting to see how people–immigrants, ex pats, travelers–adapt cuisines from other times and places to what they find available where they live. Great things often happen to food in these situations. And incidentally, if you happen to have a Neapolitan grandmother who insists that New Yorkers make their pizza wrong, tell her that we all respect her opinion on the matter, but that doesn’t mean that New York style pizza isn’t amazing. And if that grandmother is from New York, you can make the same defense of pizza from Chicago.

Pan-roasting-Pine-Nuts

 

Given that I live in the American Pacific Northwest, I’ve applied the flavors and technique used in Moroccan Chicken Tajine to local, wild-caught sockeye salmon. This takes advantage of a certain abundance available in the region of the world I live in. Wild-caught sockeye salmon is cheap and plentiful right now. It’s absolutely gorgeous. Compared to the pale, previously-frozen, farm-raised Atlantic salmon people who live in other parts of North America are used to, this fish is firm and fresh, with vibrant orange flesh. It’s also ridiculously good for you and loaded with Omega 3 fatty acids. I’m eating enough to impress a grizzly bear these days.

Skillet-Grilling-Sockeye-Salmon

Unfortunately, I don’t have a tajine (yet). I do have an enameled cast iron skillet with a lid though, so I used that. It wouldn’t quite be appropriate, then, to call my dish Salmon Tajine.  On the other hand, Salmon Cast Iron Skillet sounds rather inelegant. So let’s just call it  Moroccan Style Salmon with Olives and Preserved Lemons.

I think that this is also the point where I confess to making my own Ras El Hanout. Sorry, I don’t want to make Moroccan cuisine seem fussy. It’s really not. You can buy Ras El Hanout pre-made. If you want my recipe, let me know and I’ll send it to you.

Green-Olives-and-Preserved-Lemons

As to preparation: I think that in most stew-like applications you would likely remove the skin from the fish before cooking. However, I wanted these wild-caught sockeye salmon fillets to stay in tact, so I left the skin on. It’s a bit of a judgment call. Normally when I pan fry salmon I like to get the pan super hot so the oil shimmers and is on the verge of smoking. Then I dry the skin side well and place the fish skin side down to do most of the cooking. The skin is tough and can take some abuse while protecting the tender salmon meat it’s attached to. The salmon flesh itself is, well, a bit more delicate. In this application, however, I wanted to be able to toast and sear the Ras El Hanout on the exterior of the fish to develop the flavors and brown the flesh, so I began the searing process flesh down/skin side up. After a few moments I flipped the fillets over so the skin side was down and proceeded to add the additional ingredients.

If you give it a try, please drop me a comment and let me know how it worked out for you. If you take a picture, post it to Instagram with the hashtag #SlowBurningPassion. I’d love to see you handiwork.
